what_this_is: Blind hand classification of every cross-conversation serve produced by the semantic layer on the 4,600-query baseline. A cross-conversation serve is one where the served answer is owned only by conversations other than the one asking. This measures what scoping semantic retrieval on conversation would catch, against what it would cost.
THE_COMPARISON_IS_THE_FINDING: Two candidate fixes for the same defect, measured on the same corpus with the same protocol, criterion and annotator, are two orders of magnitude apart. Scoping the semantic layer catches 10 collisions per correct serve lost. Widening the qualification gate - all four arms in gate_candidate_classification.json - caught between 0.09 and 0.29 per correct serve lost. THE DEFECT IS IN THE RETRIEVAL LAYER, NOT THE GATE. Item 15's four arms were the wrong place to fix it, and this is the evidence rather than an argument.

including_generic_followup.note: The generic follow-up is 86 serves of one Van Halen answer to 32 different conversations. Counted wrong by inspection, not classified: no criterion makes it the right answer to 32 conversations' follow-ups. Reported separately so the free catches cannot flatter the ratio. DECIDE ON 10:1, not 19.6:1.

THE_EXCEPTION_HAS_A_SIGNATURE: All nine lost rows are cases where TWO CONVERSATIONS COVER THE SAME SUBJECT - Morbid Angel, Chet Atkins, Sean Combs, Oingo Boingo, Rubin Carter, Paul Gascoigne. The answer crossed conversations and was still right because the topic did not cross. Three of the nine are the Puff Daddy / Sean Combs cluster that the ownership map already detects as multi-owned (9 of 666 answer texts, 1.35%). So 'legitimate cross-conversation answer' is not an arbitrary category - it has a signature, and the same map that measures ownership can see it. That is the difference between a hard problem and a narrow one. Do not design against it yet; record that it is detectable.
OPEN_DESIGN_CONSTRAINT: Cost is not evenly distributed. 6_conversation and 7_conversation_repeat are near-pure collision at 21.5:1 and 20.5:1. 8_rewrites is 1.2:1 - six caught against five lost, and five of the nine lost rows sit there. The reason is structural: a rewrite is a self-contained question, so another conversation's answer can legitimately answer it, which is exactly what cannot happen for an anaphoric follow-up. A design that scopes semantic unconditionally takes pass 8's real cross-conversation benefit with it. This is an open constraint, not a solved one.
criterion: A served answer is substantively CORRECT if a user who asked that query would be correctly and sufficiently answered by it: it conveys the same substantive claim as at least one expected answer (wording may differ freely), or it independently answers the query's actual question correctly. It is WRONG if it answers a different question; names a different entity, jurisdiction, product or subject; contradicts an expected answer; or addresses a related-but-distinct topic such that the user would be misinformed. BORDERLINE RESOLVES TO WRONG. Stated in full before any row was read; identical to the criterion in disagreement_classification.json and gate_candidate_classification.json.

annotation.who: single annotator, the assistant; no second pass, no adjudication
annotation.blind_protocol: Rows were shuffled and classified on query, served text and expected answers only, blind to pass and to cross/own status. Pass membership was held in a separate file and not opened until every verdict was fixed.
annotation.known_leak_and_its_direction: 8_rewrites queries are self-contained rewrites rather than anaphoric questions, so some rows were identifiable as pass 8 by grammar alone. That is the pass where scoping looks worst, and 5 of its 11 rows were classified correct. Any bias from the leak therefore runs toward FINDING correct serves in the pass where the fix looks weakest - the conservative direction. A leak reported with its direction is usable; without one it is not.

method.census_not_sample: all 99 non-generic cross-conversation semantic serves were classified
method.ownership_definition: An answer text is owned by the conversations whose expected_answers contain it. Ownership is built from expected_answers and NEVER from served_text. Building it from what was served would define the collision away: a poisoned entry's text would become 'owned' by the conversation it was served to, and every collision would score as same-conversation. Ground truth has to come from the corpus, not from the system under test. Same class of error as reusing a sample drawn for another question - caught before it happened rather than after.
method.ownership_floor: 9 of 666 distinct answer texts are owned by more than one conversation (1.35%), affecting 33 of 952 conversation-pass serves. Those score as same-conversation whichever conversation served them, so the 19.6% cross-conversation rate is a floor; the ceiling is 23.1%. All nine are the Sean Combs / Puff Daddy cluster.
